Nicholas Ridley
NIK-uh-lus RID-lee
proper noun (figure)
Greek Nikolaos — "victory of the people" (from nikē, victory + laos, people). Apostolic and patristic Christian name. Surname Ridley from English place-name — "reed clearing" or "red clearing."

See also: Nicholas Ridley

📖 Biblical Definition

Nicholas Ridley (c. 1500 — October 16, 1555 AD) was the Reformed English bishop — sequentially of Rochester (1547) and London (1550) — whose theological precision in defining the Reformed view of the Lord's Supper provided the intellectual backbone of Thomas Cranmer's 1552 Book of Common Prayer, and who was burned with Hugh Latimer at Oxford on October 16, 1555 as the second of the three Oxford Martyrs. Born in Tynedale, Northumberland; educated at Cambridge (Pembroke College) and then Sorbonne and Louvain abroad; returned to Cambridge as Master of Pembroke College. He arrived at Reformed conviction through study of the church fathers and the early-medieval Eucharistic debates (the Berengar of Tours controversy, Ratramnus of Corbie's De Corpore et Sanguine Domini), and his sustained patristic-historical case against transubstantiation became the doctrinal foundation of the Edwardian English Reformation. Appointed Bishop of Rochester 1547; translated to Bishop of London 1550; preached the funeral sermon at Edward VI's death (1553); briefly preached at Paul's Cross against Mary I's succession; arrested at Mary's accession; condemned with Cranmer and Latimer at Oxford. As Latimer and Ridley were chained back-to-back at the stake on October 16, 1555 and the fires were lit, Latimer spoke the famous candle-speech to Ridley. Ridley died in great pain because his fire was slow to take properly; Latimer (older, frailer) died quickly in the smoke. Ridley's Brief Declaration of the Lord's Supper, written in prison shortly before his death, is one of the clearest sixteenth-century English Reformed treatments of the eucharistic question.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Reformed English bishop (c. 1500-1555 AD); Bishop of Rochester then London; the theological architect of the 1552 Book of Common Prayer's Eucharistic doctrine; burned with Hugh Latimer at Oxford on October 16, 1555.

NICHOLAS RIDLEY, proper noun. Greek Nikolaos ("victory of the people") + English place-name surname.

Reformed English bishop (c. 1500-1555 AD); Bishop of Rochester (1547) then London (1550).

Author of Brief Declaration of the Lord's Supper; provided the patristic-historical foundation for Cranmer's revised Eucharistic theology in the 1552 Prayer Book.

Burned with Hugh Latimer at Oxford on October 16, 1555.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Ridley is corrupted when he is treated as the junior partner of the more famous Cranmer and Latimer rather than as the doctrinal backbone of Cranmer's mature Eucharistic theology, when his Eucharistic argument is read as merely negative (against transubstantiation) without its positive Reformed account of Christ's spiritual presence by faith, or when his martyrdom story is reduced to the Latimer candle-speech.

expand to see more

Junior-partner misreading. The three Oxford Martyrs are sometimes presented as Cranmer (the leader), Latimer (the preacher), and Ridley (a third name). The historical record shows that Ridley, more than Cranmer, supplied the patristic and historical-theological case against transubstantiation that the Reformed English Eucharistic doctrine of the 1552 Prayer Book required. Cranmer himself recorded that it was reading Ridley on the church fathers (particularly Ratramnus) that finally settled his own move from a Lutheran-tinged sacramentology to a fully Reformed one. Ridley was not the junior figure; he was the doctrinal engine.

Negative-only Eucharistic reading. Modern Anglo-Catholic and some Lutheran critics caricature Ridley's Eucharistic theology as merely anti-Roman ('not transubstantiation'). His own positive account, in the Brief Declaration, articulated a robust Reformed doctrine of Christ's spiritual presence to the believer by faith, with the elements as God-ordained signs and seals of the covenant of grace. The 1552 Prayer Book's words of administration ('Take and eat this in remembrance that Christ died for thee, and feed on him in thy heart by faith with thanksgiving') are pure Ridley. Read the negative; do not miss the positive.
